subChunks.title: HAVING
subChunks.hookHtml: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation — it is the WHERE clause for your GROUP BY buckets.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Syntax

SELECT rank, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM   apprentices
GROUP BY rank
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

WHERE vs HAVING

ClauseWhen it runsCan filter on
WHEREBefore GROUP BYRow-level columns
HAVINGAfter GROUP BYAggregates and GROUP BY columns

Both together

SELECT rank, SUM(xp) AS total_xp
FROM   apprentices
WHERE  xp > 500           -- filter individual rows first
GROUP BY rank
HAVING SUM(xp) > 2000;   -- then filter groups

Full clause order

SELECT
FROM
WHERE       -- rows
GROUP BY
HAVING      -- groups
ORDER BY
LIMIT

storyBeats.text: A third messenger: 'Show only ranks with two or more apprentices.'

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: HAVING is WHERE for groups. You cannot use WHERE to filter on COUNT — COUNT does not exist until after GROUP BY. HAVING runs after. That is why they are two separate clauses, not one. Learn the order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Busy ranks only

Return each rank and its apprentice count (n) for ranks that have at least 2 apprentices. Order by n descending.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
SELECT rank, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM apprentices
GROUP BY rank
HAVING -- your condition here
ORDER BY n DESC;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns 1 row — only 'Apprentice' has 2 members
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (1,'Alice','Apprentice',1200),(2,'Bjorn','Adept',2400),(3,'Cassia','Mage',4800),(4,'Dorian','Novice',80),(5,'Elara','Archmage',7500),(6,'Fenrir','Apprentice',950);

guidedPracticeTests.label: The rank returned is Apprentice with n=2
guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT rank, COUNT(*) AS n FROM apprentices GROUP BY rank HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY n DESC

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Return each rank and SUM(xp) AS total_xp for ranks whose total XP exceeds 2 000. Filter individual rows to xp > 500 first (WHERE), then apply the HAVING filter.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and why you need two separate clauses rather than using WHERE for both.

questions.prompt: When does HAVING run relative to GROUP BY?
options: After GROUP BY — it filters groups based on aggregate results
Before GROUP BY — it filters rows like WHERE
At the same time as WHERE
questions.answer: After GROUP BY — it filters groups based on aggregate results
questions.explanation: HAVING is evaluated after aggregation. It can reference aggregate functions like COUNT(*) and SUM(xp) because those values exist at that point. WHERE cannot.

questions.prompt: Why does `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` cause an error when used with GROUP BY?
options: WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so COUNT(*) has not been computed yet
WHERE cannot be used with GROUP BY at all
COUNT(*) requires HAVING, not WHERE, for syntactic reasons unrelated to execution order
WHERE requires a column name, not an aggregate
questions.answer: WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so COUNT(*) has not been computed yet
questions.explanation: The engine evaluates FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING. COUNT(*) is a GROUP BY-level concept — it does not exist when WHERE is evaluated.

questions.prompt: Using lesson data, how many groups remain after `GROUP BY rank HAVING SUM(xp) > 2000`?
options: 3 (Adept 2400, Mage 4800, Archmage 7500, Apprentice 2150 — wait: Adept=2400, Mage=4800, Archmage=7500, Apprentice=2150)
4 — Adept, Mage, Archmage, Apprentice all exceed 2000
questions.answer: 4 — Adept, Mage, Archmage, Apprentice all exceed 2000
questions.explanation: Rank totals: Apprentice=1200+950=2150, Adept=2400, Mage=4800, Archmage=7500, Novice=80. The first four exceed 2000; Novice (80) does not. Four groups remain.

questions.prompt: When should you use WHERE instead of HAVING, even if both seem to work?
options: Use WHERE to filter rows before aggregation — it is faster because fewer rows reach GROUP BY
Use HAVING for everything — it is more flexible
They are interchangeable; use whichever reads more clearly
WHERE is only for numeric columns; HAVING is for text
questions.answer: Use WHERE to filter rows before aggregation — it is faster because fewer rows reach GROUP BY
questions.explanation: WHERE eliminates rows early, before the GROUP BY step. This reduces the data the engine must aggregate. HAVING runs after aggregation and cannot reduce that cost. When the condition applies to a raw column (not an aggregate), always use WHERE.
